questions.stem: A county museum is digitising its photographic archive. The scanning will be done by eighteen volunteers who come in twice a week; they are unpaid and hold no contract. The stakeholder register you inherit lists curators, the imaging supplier and the lottery funding body, but no volunteers, because your predecessor listed only people attached to a contract or a budget line. What should you do first?

options.text: Add the volunteer group to the register and analyse its interest and influence as you would any other stakeholder.
options.rationale: The volunteers do the work the project depends on and their working week changes because of it. That is what makes someone a stakeholder, and analysis is what turns the entry into an engagement decision.

options.text: Leave the register as it is, since volunteers have no contractual standing and approve nothing.
options.rationale: This confuses authority with stakeholder status. Plenty of people who sign nothing can still stop a project, and a group that can withdraw its labour overnight is a clear example.

options.text: Ask the curators to represent the volunteers' interests, since they supervise them day to day.
options.rationale: It installs a proxy nobody has agreed to and assumes supervisors know what those they supervise want. Convenient representation is the most common way a group's actual position stays invisible.

options.text: Add the volunteers to the distribution list for the weekly project update.
options.rationale: This jumps to a mechanism before any analysis exists to justify it. Choosing how to communicate with a group before knowing what they need from you is how newsletters end up unread.

questions.explanation: Identification asks whether someone affects the work or is affected by it, not whether the organisation pays them or whether they hold a decision right. Employment status, budget lines and signing authority are convenient filters and each one hides a category of people who can stop delivery. The register exists to feed analysis, so the entry is the beginning of the work rather than the end of it.
questions.mindset: Ask who the work touches, not who the organisation pays.

questions.stem: Your team builds booking software for a group of veterinary practices. The operations partner, an influential stakeholder, has asked to sit in on the daily standup each morning so she can keep up with progress. The team has said yes to be helpful, but two developers have told you privately that they will stop raising problems in front of a partner. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Offer her a mechanism that meets the need behind the request, such as a short weekly walkthrough of the board plus a standing invitation to the review, and explain what the standup is for.
options.rationale: She asked for a forum but what she wants is current information. Meeting that need elsewhere keeps the relationship and leaves the team a place where saying something is going wrong costs nothing.

options.text: Agree to her attending, on the grounds that a transparent team should have nothing to hide from stakeholders.
options.rationale: It treats transparency as an absolute and ignores what observation does to a room. The standup does not stop being transparent when it goes quiet; it just stops being useful.

options.text: Decline, explaining that the standup belongs to the team.
options.rationale: The boundary is right and the answer is incomplete. Refusing an influential stakeholder without offering an alternative reads as exclusion and spends a relationship to protect a fifteen-minute meeting.

options.text: Agree to her attending, and ask the developers to bring problems to you privately afterwards instead.
options.rationale: This keeps the event and moves the substance into a back channel. You now run two standups, only one of which is honest, and the stakeholder is watching the one that is not.

questions.explanation: A request from a stakeholder names a forum, but what it carries is a need, and those are rarely the same thing. Engagement design starts from the need and then chooses a mechanism that serves the stakeholder without damaging what the forum exists to do. Forums that depend on candour are worth protecting explicitly, because their failure is silent and looks like everything being fine.
questions.mindset: Answer the need a request carries, not the forum it names.

questions.stem: On a sample-tracking product for a seed-testing laboratory, the head of the testing floor has started messaging two developers directly with changes he wants. The items are small, they get done, and the developers rather enjoy the contact. The product owner does not know, and the sprint goal has slipped twice. His staff will use the product every day. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Find out what makes the direct route attractive to him, then agree a fast path through the product owner that keeps his items visible and prioritised.
options.rationale: People bypass a process when it is slower than their need. Removing the reason keeps the relationship and returns prioritisation to the person accountable for it.

options.text: Ask the developers to stop responding and to refer him to the product owner.
options.rationale: It enforces the rule without touching the cause, so the pressure simply moves elsewhere. It also spends a significant stakeholder's goodwill to defend a route he already finds too slow.

options.text: Add his requests to the backlog retrospectively so that the work is at least recorded.
options.rationale: This documents the bypass rather than resolving it. A backlog that records what has already been built is a log, not a plan, and prioritisation becomes a formality.

options.text: Raise it with his line manager as a breach of the agreed way of working.
options.rationale: Escalating before attempting the conversation converts a co-operative stakeholder into a wary one. He is behaving reasonably by his own lights, and nobody has yet offered him anything better.

questions.explanation: Someone routing around an agreed channel is usually reporting something true about that channel: it is too slow, too opaque, or too expensive for the size of their request. The durable response changes the route rather than policing the person, because policing works only while it is being watched. Engagement mechanisms have to be affordable for the stakeholder as well as correct for the team.
questions.mindset: When someone routes around the process, treat the route as evidence about the process.

questions.stem: You are starting a rewiring project across a further-education college. The PMO hands you the stakeholder register from the campus lighting scheme finished three years ago, saying most of it still applies. It holds thirty-one names with roles, influence ratings and preferred contact methods. Since then two departments have merged and the estates director has changed twice. What is the right use of this register?

options.text: Treat it as a source for identification, and verify every entry against the current organisation before any rating is used.
options.rationale: The hard part of identification is remembering the people who are easy to miss, and that survives. Ratings describe a moment and a different project, so they have to be re-earned before they drive anything.

options.text: Adopt it as the project's register and correct entries as changes come to light.
options.rationale: It makes three-year-old judgements the working baseline, so errors surface only when they have already cost something. You end up defending assessments you never made.

options.text: Discard it and rebuild the register from scratch through interviews.
options.rationale: This throws away genuine work to avoid a check that would take an afternoon. Starting clean feels rigorous but usually reproduces a shorter list containing only the obvious people.

options.text: Keep it for reference and record the stakeholders who turn up to the kickoff.
options.rationale: It lets attendance define the register. The stakeholders who matter most are frequently the ones with no reason to attend a kickoff and every ability to intervene later.

questions.explanation: Identification travels between projects and analysis does not. Who exists in an organisation changes slowly, but influence, interest and attitude are properties of a particular project at a particular time, and they decay quietly because nothing announces that they have. Reusing prior work is efficient precisely when the two halves are separated rather than inherited as one document.
questions.mindset: Reuse the names, re-earn the judgements.

questions.stem: A university is replacing its library management system over eighteen months. The students' union president sits on the project board and has been a consistent advocate. The post is elected annually and the handover falls in month nine, in the middle of the migration; her successor is unknown and may hold different views. A colleague suggests you simply brief whoever arrives. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree with the union now how continuity will be held across the changeover, through written positions, an induction and a permanent officer alongside the elected post.
options.rationale: The turnover date is known, so it is a planning problem rather than a surprise. Building continuity into the union's own structure means the project does not restart its case every summer.

options.text: Brief the incoming president thoroughly in month nine, using the outgoing president's notes.
options.rationale: It leaves a foreseeable break to be repaired after it opens. New postholders form a position within days, usually from whoever reaches them first, and your briefing is unlikely to be first.

options.text: Ask the current president to remain on the board after her term ends.
options.rationale: It attaches continuity to someone who will have no mandate to represent anybody. It also undercuts the successor, who now sits beside a predecessor the project treats as the real voice.

options.text: Move the board seat to a permanent member of university staff who works closely with students.
options.rationale: This buys stability by removing the stakeholder's own voice. You keep the seat filled and lose the representation it existed to provide, which is the thing the board actually needs.

questions.explanation: Where a role turns over on a known cycle, the engagement is with the office rather than with the individual currently holding it. Continuity has to live somewhere that outlasts a term: written positions, standing staff, an agreed induction. A relationship that exists only in one person's head is a relationship with an expiry date, and the date is usually in the plan already.
questions.mindset: Engage the office as well as the person holding it.

questions.stem: Six months into a hospital pathology system replacement, you notice that most design decisions have been shaped by the deputy laboratory manager, who replies within the hour and always finds time for you. The clinical director, who chairs the group that must approve the design, has met you twice and cancelled three times. The design review is in four weeks. What should you do?

options.text: Treat the gap as an engagement failure to close now, securing structured input from the clinical director before the review and recording the deputy's contribution as input rather than approval.
options.rationale: Four weeks is enough to get a decision-maker's position while the design can still absorb it. Separating input from approval also protects the deputy, who has been answering questions above her remit.

options.text: Carry on with the deputy, who knows the laboratory better, and send the director the pack a week before the review.
options.rationale: It mistakes availability for authority. The person who can reject the design meets it for the first time at the point where changing it is most expensive.

options.text: Ask the deputy to brief the clinical director on your behalf.
options.rationale: It hands your most consequential relationship to someone with neither the standing to press nor any incentive to report back that the director is unhappy.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor that the clinical director is not making himself available.
options.rationale: Escalating before exhausting the ordinary routes spends credibility and frames a senior clinician as an obstacle. It also guarantees the first thing he hears about you is a complaint.

questions.explanation: Engagement drifts towards whoever is easiest to reach, and the drift is invisible because every individual conversation feels productive. Influence is a property of the decision in question, not of responsiveness, so a periodic check on who you have actually been spending time with is worth more than any amount of good intent. Access is a convenience; authority is the thing that has to be engaged.
questions.mindset: Notice who you are talking to most, and check that it is who you should be.

questions.stem: You are three weeks into a ferry operator's ticketing replacement. You built the stakeholder register by asking the sponsor, a commercial director, to name everyone who mattered; he gave you twenty-two names and you have engaged all of them. In passing, a port supervisor mentions that nobody has spoken to the deck crews who will use the handheld scanners on every sailing. What should you conclude?

options.text: The identification method has a predictable bias, and the register needs a second, independent route into it, such as walking the process end to end and asking who touches it.
options.rationale: One informant produces one person's map, however senior or well intentioned. A method that starts from the work rather than from the org chart finds the people the org chart does not think about.

options.text: The sponsor left the crews out deliberately and should be challenged about the omission.
options.rationale: It attributes to intent something a single-source method produces on its own. Acting on that reading damages the relationship you most depend on, over a gap you created by only asking once.

options.text: The crews are users rather than stakeholders, and belong in the training plan instead.
options.rationale: A definitional dodge that reclassifies inconvenient people out of scope. Anyone whose daily work changes has both interest and the ability to make adoption fail.

options.text: The register is broadly sound and the port supervisor can speak for the crews.
options.rationale: It closes identification on the word of whoever happened to raise it, and appoints a proxy who has not agreed to the role and may not know the job in detail.

questions.explanation: Every stakeholder list carries the shape of the method that produced it, and asking one well-placed person produces a faithful copy of that person's network. The correction is not more diligence with the same method but a second route in from a different direction, typically the work itself: who handles it, who is interrupted by it, who has to change on the day it lands.
questions.mindset: Every list of stakeholders carries the shape of the person who wrote it.

questions.stem: A credit union's product team demonstrates every two weeks. The head of compliance has declined the last five invitations, saying she would rather review the whole thing once it is finished. She holds a sign-off the release cannot go without. The team reads this as disengagement, has stopped inviting her, and now refers to her as a blocker in planning. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish what she actually has to attest to, then agree a mechanism sized to it, such as a short session at each of the two or three points where a compliance decision is genuinely available.
options.rationale: It starts from her obligation rather than the team's calendar, and it creates moments where her input can still change something, which is the only kind of engagement that prevents a late refusal.

options.text: Keep inviting her to every review and escalate her non-attendance to the sponsor.
options.rationale: It treats turning up to your ceremony as the measure of engagement and escalates a preference as a failure. She is not obliged to work in fortnights because the team does.

options.text: Accept her preference and plan a single compliance review shortly before release.
options.rationale: It agrees to an arrangement that guarantees late discovery. She gets exactly one opportunity to say no, at the point where no is most expensive for everyone including her.

options.text: Send her the recording and release notes after each demonstration.
options.rationale: It substitutes volume for engagement. She receives more material and still has no point at which anything she says can alter the thing she will later be asked to sign.

questions.explanation: Cadence is part of tailoring, and the question is never whether a stakeholder will come to the team's event. It is where in their own decision cycle their input can still change the outcome, and what mechanism is proportionate to that. A stakeholder holding a gate is the one where getting this wrong is most expensive, because the cost of their absence is deferred rather than avoided.
questions.mindset: Fit the rhythm of engagement to what the stakeholder actually has to decide.

questions.stem: At every review of your food traceability tool, a quality manager lists what is wrong with the increment and rarely says anything positive. Morale dips afterwards and two developers have asked you to stop inviting her. Her comments have twice caught labelling defects that would otherwise have reached the shop floor. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep her in the room and change the format so her criticism arrives usefully, asking for specifics against agreed criteria and making the defects she has prevented visible to the team.
options.rationale: It keeps the signal and works on how it is delivered and received. Showing the team what her comments have saved converts her from an ordeal into a resource without asking her to be someone else.

options.text: Stop inviting her and take her feedback separately in writing afterwards.
options.rationale: It removes your most reliable source of early failure information from the forum where the team could act on it, and the written channel will decay within a month.

options.text: Ask her to balance her criticism with positives to protect team morale.
options.rationale: It manages the messenger rather than the reaction, and risks softening exactly the signal you need. Reviewers who are coached on tone learn to say less.

options.text: Keep inviting her but tell the team to treat her comments as advisory.
options.rationale: It preserves the appearance of engagement while removing its consequence. She will notice within two sprints, and then you have lost the input for real.

questions.explanation: A consistently critical stakeholder is the cheapest failure detection a project has, and the instinct to exclude one is strongest exactly when they are working. The task is to design the encounter so dissent arrives as usable evidence rather than as a verdict, which usually means agreed criteria, specifics rather than impressions, and a team that can see what the criticism is buying them.
questions.mindset: Protect the channel that brings you bad news early.

questions.stem: An offshore wind developer must route an export cable across farmland to a substation. Statutory consultation opens in three weeks and runs for six; your design freeze is five weeks away. Landowners on two of the three candidate routes have not been contacted, because the legal team regards the consultation as the proper mechanism for hearing them. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Engage the affected landowners before the window opens, so what they raise can still shape the route and the consultation records positions rather than discovering them.
options.rationale: It puts the contact where the design is still movable. It also means the formal process confirms an understanding both sides already have, which is what makes consultations short.

options.text: Wait for the consultation and respond formally to whatever is submitted.
options.rationale: It treats a legal minimum as the engagement strategy. Objections then arrive after the freeze, when the only available answers are refusal or an expensive change.

options.text: Ask the legal team whether the consultation can be extended to run past the design freeze.
options.rationale: It adjusts the process instead of the engagement and produces no information any earlier. A longer window over a frozen design still cannot change the design.

options.text: Brief the landowners on the chosen route once the design freeze has passed.
options.rationale: Informing people after the decision is notification dressed as engagement, and it reliably converts neutral landowners into formal objectors.

questions.explanation: Statutory consultation sets a floor for who must be heard and by when; it says nothing about when engagement is worth doing. The value of any contact with an affected stakeholder is proportional to how much of the decision is still open when it happens, which means engagement is planned backwards from the freeze rather than forwards from the legal calendar.
questions.mindset: Consult while the answer can still change; anything later is an announcement.

questions.stem: A water utility's catchment scheme depends on a river conservation charity to recruit farmers into a land-management trial. The same charity is campaigning publicly against the utility over storm overflows and has named your programme in a critical article. Your communications team wants all contact with them suspended until the campaign ends. The trial needs forty farms signed up by spring. What should the programme manager do?

options.text: Keep the delivery relationship running and handle it separately from the campaign, agreeing openly with the charity what each side can expect on each front.
options.rationale: It matches the response to the interest rather than to the organisation. Naming the separation explicitly is what stops either side treating a move on one front as a betrayal on the other.

options.text: Suspend contact until the campaign ends, as the communications team advises.
options.rationale: It collapses a stakeholder into a single position and sacrifices a delivery dependency to a reputational reflex. The campaign has no end date, and the spring deadline does.

options.text: Make continued involvement in the trial conditional on the article being withdrawn.
options.rationale: It makes delivery hostage to an editorial demand you have no standing to make, and hands the charity a much better story than the one they published.

options.text: Replace the charity with a commercial land agent for the recruitment work.
options.rationale: It discards the one asset that makes the trial credible to farmers, which is the charity's independence from the utility. Campaigning is evidence of that independence, not of unreliability.

questions.explanation: Organisations hold several interests at once and they do not have to be consistent. Analysis that resolves a stakeholder into an ally or an opponent will mis-handle anyone who is both, which in regulated and public-facing work is most of the significant ones. Working interest by interest, and saying out loud which one a given conversation belongs to, keeps a hostile position on one front from destroying co-operation on another.
questions.mindset: Analyse a stakeholder interest by interest, not as a friend or an enemy.

questions.stem: Your product improves the tooling used by an internal service desk of ninety agents. The desk sends whoever is free to each fortnightly review, so you meet different agents every time. Feedback contradicts itself between sessions and the team has begun discounting all of it. The desk manager says rotation is fair and keeps everyone involved. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree a small standing group with the manager to carry continuity, and keep the wider rotation for a different purpose such as usability sessions on specific changes.
options.rationale: It gives the feedback channel a memory while honouring the fairness concern rather than overriding it. Two mechanisms with different jobs beat one mechanism failing at both.

options.text: Ask the manager to send the same two agents to every review from now on.
options.rationale: It solves continuity by dismissing the reason the manager gave for rotating. Getting your way on this costs more than it returns, and the arrangement lapses as soon as attention moves elsewhere.

options.text: Treat the contradictions as ordinary variation and weight feedback by how often a theme recurs.
options.rationale: It treats a structural fault in the channel as statistical noise. Recurrence here measures who happened to attend, not how widely a view is held.

options.text: Replace the reviews with a survey to all ninety agents.
options.rationale: It trades depth for reach and removes the conversation where a contradiction could have been unpicked. Surveys inherit the same problem without anyone present to notice.

questions.explanation: Feedback from a group that never repeats cannot accumulate. Each session restarts the shared context, so participants answer different questions from the ones they were asked, and the team eventually protects itself by ignoring the channel. Engagement mechanisms need continuity of memory as much as breadth of coverage, and when both are genuinely wanted they usually need to be two mechanisms rather than one compromise.
questions.mindset: Feedback needs continuity of memory as much as breadth of coverage.

questions.stem: You are rolling out milk-collection scheduling software to a dairy cooperative of 340 farmer-members. The elected board tells you members are content and asks that everything be routed through them. A short survey you ran at a regional meeting found that fewer than half of those who answered knew the collection windows would change at all. The board chair is one of your strongest supporters. What should you do?

options.text: Take the finding back to the board and design a direct route to members with their agreement, in addition to the board channel rather than instead of it.
options.rationale: It treats the gap as a shared problem and uses the chair's support to fix it. Adding a channel with the board's blessing keeps the mandate intact while getting information to the people it concerns.

options.text: Accept the board's assurance, since elected representatives speak for their members.
options.rationale: It confuses the legitimacy of a mandate with the accuracy of a report. Representatives can be entirely sincere and still be describing a membership they have not asked recently.

options.text: Begin communicating directly with members and tell the board once it is under way.
options.rationale: It bypasses the structure that gives you access and converts your strongest supporter into an opponent, over a problem he has not yet been given the chance to solve.

options.text: Repeat the survey across every region before raising anything with the board.
options.rationale: It spends weeks confirming something you already have enough of to act on, and the delay falls on the members who do not know their collection times are changing.

questions.explanation: A representative body is itself a stakeholder with its own interests, and one of those interests is being the channel. What it reports is evidence about the body as much as about the people behind it, so the reach of the channel needs testing rather than assuming. The way to do that without breaking the relationship is to work through the representatives on the fix rather than around them.
questions.mindset: Trust representatives with the relationship, but verify what is reaching the people they represent.

questions.stem: Your internal payments platform serves eleven engineering teams. The quarterly stakeholder survey drew four responses, nobody attends the open office hour, and yet during every incident your channel fills with detailed complaints about the same two interfaces. The platform team has concluded that its stakeholders are disengaged and wants the engineering director to mandate attendance. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat the incident traffic and usage data as the channel that is already working, and go to the teams on their terms, at their own ceremonies, about the two interfaces they keep naming.
options.rationale: It reads engagement from behaviour rather than from attendance, and moves the cost of contact onto the party who wants something. The two named interfaces are a free agenda.

options.text: Ask the engineering director to make the office hour compulsory for each team.
options.rationale: It compels presence and obtains compliance instead of information. It also blames stakeholders for the failure of a mechanism they never agreed to.

options.text: Conclude that the platform is broadly meeting needs, since only incidents generate comment.
options.rationale: It reads silence as satisfaction when the more likely explanation is that the cost of speaking up exceeds the benefit until something breaks.

options.text: Replace the survey with a longer one covering every interface.
options.rationale: It doubles down on an instrument with a four-response return. More questions to a population that is not answering produces less data, not more.

questions.explanation: Non-response is information about the channel before it is information about the stakeholders. Where people already spend attention, whether that is an incident thread, a support queue or usage telemetry, there is an engagement channel operating whether or not anyone designed it. Meeting stakeholders inside their existing rituals costs them nothing and is usually the difference between compliance and contribution.
questions.mindset: When nobody answers, change the channel before you judge the audience.

questions.stem: Your programme upgrades a city transport authority's fare system. The cabinet member who must approve the operating model engages only through a policy adviser, who has attended every meeting and assures you the member is content. Three weeks ago the member made a public remark about fare capping that contradicts the approved model. The adviser says it was a misspeak and asks you not to make anything of it. What should you do?

options.text: Treat the remark as evidence about what has actually reached the member, and seek a documented confirmation of the operating model through a route the adviser can support and be part of.
options.rationale: It tests the channel against the principal's own behaviour without going behind the person who controls access. Keeping the adviser inside the fix is what makes the confirmation obtainable.

options.text: Accept the adviser's explanation, given that he has been reliable and is the agreed channel.
options.rationale: It takes a filter's account of its own filtering as evidence about the principal. The one thing an intermediary cannot report is what they have not passed on.

options.text: Write to the cabinet member directly, setting out the contradiction and asking for clarification.
options.rationale: It goes around the agreed channel in a political environment, embarrasses the adviser, and is likely to reach the member framed as a complaint by the person you bypassed.

options.text: Pause the operating model workstream until the member's position has been clarified publicly.
options.rationale: It converts an uncertainty about engagement into a delivery stoppage before any attempt to resolve it, and makes the programme the story rather than the fare policy.

questions.explanation: Where a stakeholder is reachable only through an intermediary, the intermediary's assurances are the one form of evidence that cannot confirm itself. Verification has to come from what the principal does and says in the open: decisions taken, documents signed, positions stated publicly. When those diverge from the assurances, the right move is usually to make the principal's position explicit through a route the intermediary can endorse rather than to circumvent them.
questions.mindset: Check a proxy against what the principal does, not against what the proxy says.

questions.stem: Your sponsor, the finance director of a merging college group, tells you to stop meeting the head of curriculum, whom she calls obstructive and unnecessary to any decision. The head of curriculum owns the timetabling data your migration depends on, and her team is due to do the data cleansing in six weeks. You have found her demanding but co-operative. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Go back to the sponsor with the dependency, agree who holds the relationship and on what terms, and keep the working contact the data requires.
options.rationale: It gives the sponsor the delivery consequence of her instruction, which she may not have known, and settles ownership of a relationship rather than leaving it ambiguous.

options.text: Comply, and obtain the timetabling data through the sponsor's office instead.
options.rationale: It accepts an instruction that severs a delivery dependency and routes technical work through a political channel, where it will arrive slowly and without the detail cleansing needs.

options.text: Keep meeting her as before, and stop mentioning the contact in reports.
options.rationale: It protects delivery by concealing it. When it surfaces, and it will, you lose the sponsor's trust and the relationship you were protecting in the same afternoon.

options.text: Ask the sponsor's own director to overrule the instruction.
options.rationale: It escalates over the sponsor's head on a first disagreement, spending the one relationship a project manager cannot rebuild, before any attempt to discuss it.

questions.explanation: Sponsors set direction and are entitled to views about people, but an instruction that removes a dependency is a decision about delivery whether or not it was framed that way. The obligation is to return the consequence to whoever issued the instruction, in concrete terms with dates attached, and to settle who will hold the relationship instead. Silent compliance and silent non-compliance both leave the sponsor deciding without the facts.
questions.mindset: When an instruction removes a dependency, take the dependency back to whoever gave the instruction.

questions.stem: A joint venture is building a €140 million desalination plant. Your firm leads delivery; the partner firm holds the client relationship. The partner's project manager insists all contact with the client's operations team goes through him. Three requests for a meeting have gone unanswered in five weeks, and your commissioning plan needs their shift patterns within a fortnight. The JV agreement says nothing about access. What should you do?

options.text: Raise it through JV governance with both firms' leadership as an unmet delivery dependency with a date attached, and propose an access protocol both sides sign up to.
options.rationale: It treats access as the contractual gap it is and fixes it at the level that can, while keeping the request factual rather than personal. A protocol also protects the next twelve requests.

options.text: Contact the client's operations team directly and copy the partner's project manager for transparency.
options.rationale: It breaks a working arrangement unilaterally in a relationship governed by a contract you cannot afford to sour, and the courtesy copy makes it a deliberate breach rather than an oversight.

options.text: Build the commissioning plan on assumed shift patterns and confirm them later.
options.rationale: It substitutes an assumption for an input on the critical path, and moves discovery into commissioning, which is the most expensive place on the programme to be wrong.

options.text: Tell the client's sponsor that the partner firm is obstructing access to their own staff.
options.rationale: It exports an internal venture dispute to the customer and makes the JV look incapable of managing itself, which damages both firms including yours.

questions.explanation: When another party controls access to a stakeholder you depend on, access is a governance term rather than a favour, and silence in the agreement is a gap to be closed rather than permission to improvise. Escalating it as a dependency with a date keeps the conversation about delivery instead of about personalities, and produces a protocol that survives the individuals currently in post.
questions.mindset: Treat access to stakeholders as something to be agreed formally, not assumed or taken.

questions.stem: Your stakeholder register is reviewed at the end of each quarter. Two weeks after the last review, the finance controller of a timber processing group, whom you rated low influence and who has shown no interest in your kiln automation project, was appointed to the group investment committee. That committee will decide the capital release for your second phase. Nothing else has changed. What should you do?

options.text: Re-analyse him now and adjust the approach accordingly, and add appointments of this kind to the events that trigger a review between the quarterly ones.
options.rationale: It fixes the individual case and the process that missed it. Without the second half, the next appointment lands in the same ten-week blind spot.

options.text: Record the appointment and revisit his rating at the next quarterly review.
options.rationale: It lets a calendar govern a change that has already happened, so ten weeks of engagement runs against a rating you know to be wrong.

options.text: Raise his influence rating in the register and carry on as before.
options.rationale: It updates the document without changing anything the document exists to drive. An accurate register that alters no behaviour is bookkeeping.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to brief the investment committee so that no change of approach is needed.
options.rationale: It assumes advocacy at committee level substitutes for a relationship with a member who is indifferent, and indifference at a funding decision usually reads as scepticism.

questions.explanation: Periodic review catches slow drift; it is poorly suited to step changes, which is what appointments, reorganisations and contract awards are. A review cadence therefore needs event triggers alongside it, and the events worth listing are the ones that alter someone's power or interest without altering anything visible on your project. The output of any re-analysis is a change in what you do, not a change in a cell.
questions.mindset: Let events, not the calendar, decide when analysis is out of date.

questions.stem: A charity's fundraising director asks for a short written summary each Friday. Your team says everything is already on the shared board, updated live, and that a weekly write-up is duplicated effort the sprint cannot absorb. You check the access logs: she has not opened the board since it was shared with her in month one. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Provide the summary in the form she will actually read, kept small enough to be sustainable each week.
options.rationale: It accepts that the point is arrival rather than availability, and controls the cost by fixing the size. A short predictable note is cheaper than the misunderstandings it prevents.

options.text: Arrange training so she can use the board like everyone else.
options.rationale: It asks the stakeholder to change to suit the team's tool, and treats a preference as a competence problem. She has not asked for access; she has asked for a summary.

options.text: Decline, and send her a link to the board every Friday instead.
options.rationale: It complies in form while ignoring the request. A link is not a summary, and the logs already tell you what she will do with it.

options.text: Ask her to attend the review instead, where the same information is shown.
options.rationale: It answers a request about format with an invitation to a forum. She asked for something she can read on her own schedule, which is not what a demonstration provides.

questions.explanation: Transparency makes information available; engagement is concerned with whether it arrives. A radiator that a stakeholder never looks at has not failed technically, and that is exactly why the gap goes unnoticed. Tailoring the format to the reader is ordinary engagement work rather than an indulgence, and the sustainable version is usually smaller than the one first proposed.
questions.mindset: Information that is available but never read has not been communicated.

questions.stem: After a reorganisation at a postal sorting hub, two managers each believe they own the sorting operation your automation project will change. Both have signed off different versions of the operational acceptance criteria. Testing begins in three weeks and needs one agreed set. Neither has an updated job description and the reorganisation is still settling. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Put it to whoever both report into as a decision-rights question, with the specific conflicting criteria and the date the answer is needed.
options.rationale: It routes an ownership question to the only level that can settle it, and makes it answerable by attaching the concrete conflict and a deadline rather than a general complaint.

options.text: Merge the two sets into a single document that satisfies both managers.
options.rationale: It buys quiet by widening scope and leaves ownership unresolved, so the same argument returns at acceptance with a bigger test suite attached.

options.text: Work to the criteria signed by the more senior of the two managers.
options.rationale: It settles authority by rank rather than by mandate, and in a fresh reorganisation seniority is a poor guide to who will own the operation next month.

options.text: Wait for the reorganisation to settle and test against the original baseline meanwhile.
options.rationale: It treats an unresolved decision right as something time will fix, while testing proceeds against criteria that nobody currently owns.

questions.explanation: Two signatures on incompatible documents is a worse position than none, because it looks like agreement in the record. Ambiguous decision rights are escalated as governance questions rather than resolved by the project manager's own judgement about who seems more important, and they are answerable only when posed concretely: this conflict, these options, this date.
questions.mindset: Get decision rights settled by the people who can settle them, and put a date on it.

questions.stem: The commercial director of a hotel chain attends every review of your new booking engine, praises the team publicly and forwards the demo recordings to the board. Over four months you have asked her three times whether loyalty pricing is in the first release. Each time she says the team should do whatever it thinks best. Release scope must be fixed next week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Put the decision to her in a form that can only be answered one way or the other: the two options, what each costs, the date, and what will happen by default if no answer comes.
options.rationale: It changes the shape of the ask rather than repeating it, and a stated default makes silence into a decision she can see herself making. Written confirmation closes it.

options.text: Take her at her word, let the team decide, and record the decision in the log.
options.rationale: It accepts a delegation that was never made explicit from someone who will still own the consequence. The disagreement surfaces after release, when it is a complaint rather than a choice.

options.text: Escalate to the board, which has been watching the demonstrations.
options.rationale: It goes over an engaged and supportive stakeholder before she has been asked the question in a decidable form, and turns an ally into someone who was reported upwards.

options.text: Keep raising it at each review until she gives an answer.
options.rationale: It repeats a mechanism that has already failed three times. Asking the same question in the same forum is persistence, not a new approach.

questions.explanation: Warmth is easy to mistake for engagement because it is pleasant and highly visible. The measurable output of a stakeholder relationship is decisions taken, information given and obstacles removed, so a relationship producing none of those needs work regardless of how it feels. When a decision will not land, the thing to vary is the form of the ask, and a stated default converts an indefinite silence into a choice.
questions.mindset: Judge engagement by what a stakeholder decides, not by how they speak about you.

questions.stem: Your bakery's oven control upgrade depends on a supplier whose account manager insists every question comes through him. His replies take four days, and twice they have been technically wrong, causing three weeks of rework between them. He is protective of his engineers' time and of the commercial relationship. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Propose an agreed technical channel alongside the commercial one, so engineers speak to engineers while he keeps commercial matters, and put it to him as something that protects his position.
options.rationale: It separates two kinds of traffic that need different people and different speeds, and it is framed so the gatekeeper gains rather than loses, which is what makes it stick.

options.text: Continue through him and add contingency to allow for the four-day turnaround.
options.rationale: It prices in a defect instead of removing it, and budgets for the delay while ignoring the errors, which are what actually cost the three weeks.

options.text: Contact the supplier's engineers directly using details from an earlier project.
options.rationale: It bypasses a contractual counterpart without agreement. The answers arrive faster and the relationship you will need at every future variation is damaged.

options.text: Raise a formal complaint with the supplier's management about response times.
options.rationale: It escalates a working arrangement that has not yet been discussed, and makes the person you depend on daily defensive about something he thinks he is doing well.

questions.explanation: A single channel carrying both commercial and technical traffic will be slow and lossy, because the person holding it is optimising for a relationship rather than for accuracy and is translating material they do not fully understand. Separating the channels by agreement, with the gatekeeper's interests explicitly protected, is faster than going around them and survives the next contract negotiation.
questions.mindset: Separate the commercial channel from the technical one before either becomes a bottleneck.

questions.stem: A new in-cab routing system goes live for 120 refuse collection drivers across four depots. Drivers start at 5.30am, have no work email and are on the road by 6.15. Your engagement plan offers a monthly webinar and a project newsletter; no driver has attended one or opened the other. The depot managers tell you the drivers simply are not interested. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Rebuild the mechanism around how they actually work: short briefings in the yard at the start of a shift, delivered with their own supervisors, and a route for questions that needs no computer.
options.rationale: It puts the engagement where the audience already is, at a time they are already standing still. Using supervisors borrows credibility the project does not yet have.

options.text: Ask the depot managers to require attendance at the webinar.
options.rationale: It mandates a mechanism that does not fit the working day, so it buys resentment and produces no information. Compulsory attendance also ends any chance of honest questions.

options.text: Accept the managers' explanation and engage the drivers through them instead.
options.rationale: It adopts an explanation that blames the audience, and relies on proxies who have already demonstrated they misread the group.

options.text: Send the newsletter as a text message instead, with the same content.
options.rationale: It changes the pipe but not the shape. A one-way newsletter is still one-way, and it now arrives while the driver is mid-round.

questions.explanation: When a group ignores every channel offered, the design is the first suspect, not the group. Engagement mechanisms have to fit the stakeholder's working conditions, which for shift and field workers usually means brief, spoken, at a fixed point in an existing routine, and carried by someone they already trust. Non-participation is nearly always cheaper to explain by the mechanism than by the motives of a hundred people.
questions.mindset: Design engagement around the stakeholder's day, not around the office's.

questions.stem: Your only user representative on a hospital pharmacy dispensing product is a senior technician seconded to the team for one day a week. Her line manager has cancelled that day in six of the last eight weeks. The team has been making assumptions to keep moving, and the backlog now carries eleven items marked as needing pharmacy input. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat the single point of representation as the risk it is: agree a named deputy and a minimum commitment with the line manager, evidenced by what the eleven blocked items are costing.
options.rationale: It fixes the fragility rather than the week, and gives the line manager a concrete reason to protect the time. A deputy also means one person's diary no longer gates a stakeholder group.

options.text: Escalate the cancelled days to the sponsor as a resource problem.
options.rationale: It frames a representation problem as a staffing complaint. Even if the sponsor wins the day back, the group's voice still depends entirely on one person turning up.

options.text: Let the team make its best assumptions and validate them all at the next review.
options.rationale: It builds on assumptions and defers validation to the point where the rework is largest, which in dispensing is also where the safety consequences are.

options.text: Ask the technician to work through the eleven items by email in her own time.
options.rationale: It solves the project's problem by transferring unpaid work to a stakeholder, which is exactly where goodwill runs out and the relationship quietly ends.

questions.explanation: A single representative is a single point of failure for an entire stakeholder group's voice, and the failure mode is not refusal but ordinary competing priorities. The remedy has two parts: redundancy, so the group is still represented when one diary collapses, and an explicit mandate agreed with whoever controls that person's time, supported by evidence of what the absence costs.
questions.mindset: One person's diary should never be the only route to a stakeholder group.

questions.stem: Two departments at a port authority, vessel operations and terminal planning, have merged during your berth scheduling project. Your register lists nine stakeholders across the two, several with overlapping interests, and three of the nine have since left. The new department head has asked you what she needs from her. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Rebuild the entries around the interests that still exist, then confirm with the new head who now holds each one.
options.rationale: Interests survive a merger even when the people and titles do not, so they are the stable thing to reason from. Confirming with the head turns your reconstruction into her agreement.

options.text: Use her offer to agree how decisions will be taken and who signs what, while she is willing to set it.
options.rationale: A new postholder's first weeks are the cheapest moment to establish decision rights, because nothing has calcified yet and she is looking for ways to be useful.

options.text: Remove the three departed stakeholders and reassign their interests to their successors.
options.rationale: It assumes an interest transfers with a job title. Successors inherit a role, not a position, and a merger frequently splits one predecessor's concerns across two people.

options.text: Keep both departments' entries as they are until the merger settles, so no information is lost.
options.rationale: It preserves a register describing an organisation that no longer exists, and leaves the project working from two versions of the truth at once.

options.text: Ask the new head to nominate a single point of contact for the project.
options.rationale: It is comfortable for the project manager and funnels a merged department's several distinct interests through one person, which is how the quieter ones disappear.

questions.explanation: A structural change re-opens analysis at the level of interests rather than names, because interests are what survive a reorganisation and titles are what do not. It also creates a short window in which a new postholder is unusually willing to settle how the project and the department will work together, and that window closes as soon as their own priorities take shape.
questions.mindset: Track interests through a reorganisation; names and titles will not carry them for you.

questions.stem: Your team opened a public beta of an angling licence portal. Ninety-four people signed up, the feedback is enthusiastic and satisfaction scores are high. Almost all of them came from an online forum for keen anglers. The licence is bought by around 900,000 people a year, most of them once. Your product owner wants to treat the beta as validation and go to full release. Which two actions should the team take?

options.text: Recruit a small number of participants who match the once-a-year, low-confidence buyers the forum group does not represent.
options.rationale: It targets the population that is missing rather than enlarging the one you have. A handful of first-time buyers will surface problems ninety-four enthusiasts cannot see.

options.text: Check the beta findings against behavioural data such as drop-off points and abandoned purchases.
options.rationale: What people say and what they do are separate evidence, and abandonment data comes from everyone who tried rather than only from those who chose to comment.

options.text: Grow the beta to several hundred users recruited the same way.
options.rationale: It scales the sample without changing its bias. More of the same population produces tighter agreement about the wrong thing and raises confidence in it.

options.text: Release, and rely on support tickets after launch to reveal the problems.
options.rationale: It moves discovery to the most expensive point, through a channel that only confident users bother to use, so the group you are worried about stays silent.

options.text: Weight the satisfaction scores by how often each participant buys a licence.
options.rationale: It applies a statistical correction to a sample that contains none of the missing group. You cannot reweight your way to data you never collected.

questions.explanation: A self-selected group answers reliably about itself and about nobody else, and enthusiasm is the trait that selected them. Representativeness is a property of how participants were recruited rather than of how many there are, so the fix is always to go and find the absent segment. Pairing what a sample says with what the whole population does is the cheapest available check on both.
questions.mindset: Ask who is missing from the feedback before you ask what the feedback says.

questions.stem: Halfway through a glassworks furnace automation programme, your control systems supplier is acquired by a group that also owns your client's largest competitor. The engineers embedded in your project office are unchanged and the contract has not moved. Your client's operations director has heard about the acquisition and is uneasy, though she has not said what she wants done. Which two actions should the programme manager take?

options.text: Re-analyse the supplier as a stakeholder under new ownership: whose interests they now serve, what reports upward, and what has genuinely changed.
options.rationale: Ownership alters interests even when faces and contracts stay put, and you cannot reassure anyone credibly until you know which parts of the concern are real.

options.text: Go to the client's operations director with what you have established, before her unease hardens into a stated position.
options.rationale: An uneasy stakeholder is far easier to work with than one who has committed to a view in front of colleagues. Reaching her early is the whole opportunity.

options.text: Remove the supplier's engineers from the project office as a precaution.
options.rationale: It acts on an unassessed risk in the most visible way possible, damaging delivery and confirming to everyone that there is something to worry about.

options.text: Wait until the acquisition completes, since nothing has legally changed yet.
options.rationale: It uses legal status to defer engagement while the stakeholder's view is forming now. Positions are set during the uncertainty, not at completion.

options.text: Obtain a confidentiality undertaking from the supplier and treat the matter as closed.
options.rationale: It reaches for a document as a substitute for a conversation, and answers a relationship concern with a legal instrument the director never asked for.

questions.explanation: A change of ownership changes a supplier's interests, its reporting lines and what information now flows to whom, none of which is visible in an unchanged contract or an unchanged team. It also creates a window in which an affected stakeholder's concern is still a feeling rather than a position, and views are far cheaper to inform before they have been said out loud to other people.
questions.mindset: When ownership changes, re-read the interests before you reassure anyone.

questions.stem: Nine months into a tram extension, the sponsor cuts the £74,000 community liaison post to cover a signalling overrun. Two residents' groups, a primary school and a market traders' association currently deal with that officer every week, and construction reaches their street next month. The sponsor says the project manager can absorb the work. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Set out for the sponsor what the removed capacity actually does and what the project will stop doing if it is absorbed, naming the groups and the dates.
options.rationale: It converts a budget decision into an informed one by attaching the specific consequences, which the sponsor cannot weigh while the cost is described only as a post.

options.text: Re-prioritise the remaining engagement effort onto the stakeholders whose exposure is imminent, and tell the others what is changing for them.
options.rationale: Reduced capacity has to be allocated deliberately by exposure, and telling the deprioritised groups keeps a reduction from being experienced as being dropped.

options.text: Absorb the work personally and keep contact at its current level.
options.rationale: It accepts an unfunded commitment. Engagement is the first thing to slip under pressure and it slips silently, so the sponsor never learns the decision had a cost.

options.text: Hand the weekly contact to the construction contractor's site manager.
options.rationale: It transfers a relationship to someone whose incentives are programme and cost, with no mandate to speak for the authority and no time when the street work starts.

options.text: Suspend community contact until the signalling overrun is resolved.
options.rationale: It goes quiet at the exact moment exposure peaks, which is reliably how scattered complaints turn into an organised campaign.

questions.explanation: When engagement capacity is cut, the choice is not whether less will be done but who decides what stops. Absorbing the work silently hands that decision to whatever slips first under pressure, and the answer is always the relationships with no immediate deadline. Making the reduction explicit gives the sponsor an informed choice and gives the affected groups a change they can plan around.
questions.mindset: If capacity is cut, decide what stops rather than letting it be decided by whatever slips first.

questions.stem: Your fortnightly review falls on the last Friday of the month. The five garden centre branch managers who are your main stakeholders have missed the last three, because that is when they do month-end stock counts. They have told you they want to attend and have asked whether anything can be done about the timing. Which two actions should the team take?

options.text: Move the review to a slot that clears month-end, agreed with the managers.
options.rationale: The obstacle is a diary clash the stakeholders have already identified and offered to help solve. Removing it costs nothing and restores the input the review exists for.

options.text: Check the rest of the engagement calendar for the same clash before it repeats elsewhere.
options.rationale: Month-end will collide with anything else scheduled near it, so fixing the pattern once is cheaper than discovering it separately at every touchpoint.

options.text: Record the review and send it to the managers to watch afterwards.
options.rationale: It converts a two-way session into a broadcast when a simple scheduling change was available, and recorded demonstrations gather no feedback.

options.text: Ask each branch manager to send a deputy on those dates.
options.rationale: It substitutes attendance for the people whose judgement you need, to preserve a date that nobody is attached to.

options.text: Keep the date and log their absence in the engagement record as a risk.
options.rationale: It documents a problem that has been handed to you with its solution attached, which turns the log into a record of things nobody fixed.

questions.explanation: Repeated non-attendance usually has a structural cause, and stakeholders who ask whether the timing can change are telling you what it is. Engagement design starts from the other side's calendar and working pattern, and finding a clash once is worth checking against every other touchpoint before it recurs unnoticed somewhere else.
questions.mindset: Check the other side's calendar before you conclude they are not interested.

questions.stem: You take over a national park visitor management programme. There is a well-written stakeholder engagement plan from month two: sixteen stakeholders, tailored approaches, named owners. Nobody has updated it in six months, three of the named owners have left the programme, and the wardens' union, rated high influence in the plan itself, has not been contacted since. Which two actions should the programme manager take?

options.text: Establish where each of the sixteen actually stands today, beginning with the ones the plan itself rated highest.
options.rationale: The plan's own analysis is the best available guide to where to spend the first fortnight, and current positions are the input every other decision depends on.

options.text: Reattach owners to relationships and set a review rhythm the programme will realistically keep, however light.
options.rationale: Unowned relationships decay by default. A light cadence that survives contact with a busy month beats a thorough one that lapses again in six weeks.

options.text: Rewrite the plan from scratch, since a six-month-old plan cannot be trusted.
options.rationale: It discards analysis that is largely still sound and spends the first weeks producing a document instead of making contact with people who have not heard from the programme in half a year.

options.text: Write to all sixteen with an introduction from the new programme manager.
options.rationale: It looks diligent and treats every stakeholder identically, which is the opposite of what the plan was for. It also answers nobody's actual question.

options.text: Report the lapse to the sponsor as an inherited issue before taking any action.
options.rationale: It books the problem to a predecessor before doing anything about it, buying distance rather than progress and starting your tenure with an accusation.

questions.explanation: An engagement plan decays because relationships move, not because the document degrades, so recovery means re-establishing current positions rather than rewriting the artefact. The three things that keep it alive are named ownership of each relationship, a review rhythm modest enough to survive a bad month, and prioritisation taken from the analysis already done rather than from whoever writes to you first.
questions.mindset: An engagement plan nobody maintains becomes a record of intentions, not a description of relationships.

questions.stem: You are preparing the stakeholder analysis for a rail depot upgrade and three separate questions have come up in the same week. Your PMO has offered you a menu of techniques without saying which one answers what, and the team has started using the same grid for everything. Match each question to the technique that answers it directly. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Which of thirty-one stakeholders should receive most of your limited engagement time, given how much each can affect the outcome and how much each currently cares about it.
Whether a vocal group's claim on your attention rests on power, on a legitimate stake, or only on the urgency they attach to it themselves.
How far each stakeholder's present attitude sits from where the project needs it to be, so you can see which relationships need work and which are already sufficient.

options.text: Power and interest grid
options.rationale: Two axes that between them predict who can disrupt you and who will bother to engage, which is exactly the pair you need when allocating scarce attention across a long register.

options.text: Salience model, reading power, legitimacy and urgency separately
options.rationale: Separating the three attributes stops a loud claim being mistaken for a strong one, and shows whether a group demanding immediate attention has any standing behind the demand.

options.text: Engagement assessment matrix, current position against desired
options.rationale: It records where each stakeholder is and where they need to be, so the output is a set of gaps to work on rather than a static description of attitudes.

options.text: Responsibility assignment matrix
options.rationale: Not used. It allocates responsibility for activities and deliverables, so it answers who does the work rather than how much attention a stakeholder warrants or how they feel about the project.

questions.explanation: Each analysis technique answers one question well and the others badly, and the common failure is adopting a single favourite grid and forcing every question through it. Choosing the instrument after stating the question keeps the output usable, because the shape of the technique determines what the analysis can tell you and what it will quietly leave out.
questions.mindset: Choose the analysis that answers the question you actually have.

questions.stem: Three things have happened on your water utility programme in the same fortnight. Each changes something you hold in writing, and your PMO has asked which document you will update first in each case, because everything has lately been landing in the issue log by default. Match each event to the artefact that has to change first. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The regulator appoints a named case officer to your programme; until now you had no individual contact there at all.
You establish that a director who was supportive has turned resistant since her division's capital budget was cut.
A stakeholder tells you the fortnightly update reaches her on Tuesday, a day after the meeting where she would use it.

options.text: The stakeholder register: a newly identified individual, their role and their initial assessment
options.rationale: A person who did not exist in your analysis now does, and identification precedes everything else. Until the entry exists, no engagement approach can be planned for them.

options.text: The engagement approach for that stakeholder: current position, desired position and what will move it
options.rationale: The change is in attitude rather than identity, which is what this artefact tracks. It also forces the useful question of what specific action is expected to close the new gap.

options.text: The communications approach: the timing, format and route of what she receives
options.rationale: Nothing about who she is or where she stands has changed; the delivery is simply mistimed, and timing is what this artefact exists to set.

options.text: The issue log: an entry describing the problem, its owner and a target date
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three is yet an issue needing resolution, and logging them here would record that something happened without changing the plan anyone works from.

questions.explanation: Different artefacts carry different kinds of decision: who exists, where they stand, and what they receive when. Putting a change in the wrong one is not a filing error, because each document is read by different people for different purposes, and a change recorded where nobody acts on it has the same effect as not recording it at all.
questions.mindset: Put a change where it will be acted on, not merely where it will be recorded.

questions.stem: Your product organisation is agreeing who holds which stakeholder relationship, because three of them have been drifting between people and nobody is sure who called last. Your sponsor is a divisional director, and the team includes several senior engineers and a product owner. For each relationship below, choose who is best placed to hold it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A director in a peer division who has begun arguing in executive meetings that your product duplicates something his own team already builds.
The lead engineer at a partner firm whose integration release timings your team needs to know every sprint.
The day-to-day prioritisation conversation with the operations manager whose staff use the product all day.

options.text: Your sponsor, director to director
options.rationale: A dispute conducted between peers at executive level can only be answered at that level. A project manager arguing the point lacks both the standing and the room to be heard.

options.text: A named engineer on your team, engineer to engineer
options.rationale: The contact is technical, frequent and detailed, so it belongs with people who speak the same language daily rather than being relayed through anyone.

options.text: The product owner
options.rationale: Prioritisation is the product owner's accountability, so holding the conversation that feeds it keeps the decision and the relationship in the same pair of hands.

options.text: The PMO, through its standard reporting cycle
options.rationale: Not used. Reporting keeps people informed but cannot hold a relationship, and the PMO has neither the standing for the first case nor the context for the other two.

questions.explanation: Relationships are held at the level with matching standing and at the frequency the contact actually needs, which means a project manager who owns all of them personally is a bottleneck in the easy cases and out of their depth in the hard ones. Naming an owner for each relationship is what stops the awkward ones drifting until nobody has spoken to that stakeholder for a month.
questions.mindset: Match the relationship to the person with standing to hold it, not to whoever carries the project title.

questions.stem: Your livestock traceability programme has forty-one stakeholders on the register and you have roughly six hours a week for engagement. Reviewing the last month, you find that time has been allocated largely by who asked most insistently rather than by the analysis you did in month one. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A stakeholder with high interest in the outcome but no authority over it has begun asking for a weekly one-to-one, which you could not sustain across the register. You should
A stakeholder you rated high influence and low interest has ignored two invitations and does not open the update, but could halt the rollout at the trading standards gate. You should

options.text: give him a regular lower-cost route that keeps him genuinely informed, and reserve your direct time for the decisions he is actually part of
options.rationale: High interest is best served by reliable information rather than by your calendar. Offering a real alternative rather than a refusal keeps an engaged supporter engaged.

options.text: work out the few points where her influence actually lands, and approach her about those specifically
options.rationale: Someone with low interest will not respond to general contact, but will respond to the narrow question that touches their own accountability. That is the only opening you have.

options.text: remove them from the engagement plan and re-engage only if they raise something themselves
options.rationale: Not used. Neither lack of authority nor lack of attendance is grounds for dropping a stakeholder: the first cares and will act on what he hears, and the second can stop the rollout without ever attending anything.

questions.explanation: Analysis earns its keep by deciding where scarce attention goes, and the failure mode is allocating it by volume of request instead, which systematically over-serves the enthusiastic and under-serves the dangerous. High interest is generally answered with good information at low cost, while high influence is answered with targeted contact at the specific points where that influence is exercised.
questions.mindset: Let the analysis, not the volume of the request, decide where your hours go.

questions.stem: Your merger integration programme keeps its stakeholder register on a site any employee of either publishing house can open. Two entries describe named directors as resistant, and one records that a stakeholder is expected to lose her role in the new structure. A colleague has suggested softening the wording so that nothing would cause offence if read. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: When one of those directors asks you directly how he is described in the register, you should
For assessments that are candid but sensitive, such as an expected role loss, the programme should

options.text: tell him plainly how his position is recorded, and use the conversation to test whether the assessment is actually right
options.rationale: An assessment you cannot defend to its subject is probably wrong, and being asked is a rare chance to correct it. Evasion here costs more trust than the entry ever could.

options.text: hold them in a restricted part of the register with named access, keeping the shared version factual
options.rationale: Access control answers the sensitivity without degrading the analysis, and information about someone's job security has an obvious reason to be handled narrowly.

options.text: reword the assessments so that nothing in them would embarrass anyone who read them
options.rationale: Not used. Writing analysis for an imagined reader rather than for the decision it informs empties it out: a register that cannot say a stakeholder is resistant cannot help anyone plan for resistance.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis is only useful while it is candid, and candour is only safe while its circulation is controlled, so the two requirements are met by different means. Diluting the words to make a document universally readable destroys the analysis and does not even achieve discretion, because a vague record still signals that an assessment exists. Where a subject asks directly, honesty tends to improve the assessment as well as the relationship.
questions.mindset: Write the assessment you actually need, then control who can read it.

questions.stem: You are running a catering contract change across a multi-academy trust and maintain an engagement assessment matrix using five levels: unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive and leading. Current positions are the trust finance lead supportive, the catering supplier neutral, the parents forum resistant, one head of school unaware, and the kitchen staff representative supportive. The desired positions, in the same order, are supportive, supportive, neutral, supportive and leading.

blanks.label: How many of the five stakeholders are already at their desired position
blanks.rationale: Only the trust finance lead is where the project needs her, supportive against a desired supportive. The other four each show a gap, including the kitchen staff representative, whose supportive rating is still one level short of leading.

blanks.label: How many levels the head of school must move, counting the five levels as successive steps
blanks.rationale: From unaware to supportive is three steps on the scale: unaware to resistant to neutral to supportive. It is the largest single move in the matrix and the least likely to be achieved by a written update.

blanks.label: Which stakeholder needs opposition reduced rather than enthusiasm increased
blanks.rationale: The parents forum is the only stakeholder recorded as resistant, and its desired position is neutral rather than supportive, so the aim is to remove an obstacle rather than to win an advocate.

questions.explanation: The value of this matrix is in the distance between the two columns rather than in either column alone, and the desired position is a judgement that should differ by stakeholder. Setting everyone's target to supportive wastes effort on people whose neutrality is sufficient and hides the cases where mere support is not enough because the project needs someone to argue its case for it.
questions.mindset: Decide what each stakeholder actually needs to become, not how enthusiastic you would like them to be.

questions.stem: Your team surveyed the 240 staff who will use a new shift-swapping app. Fifty-four replied, and forty-two of those rated the current process poor. The product owner wants to tell the steering group that 78 percent of staff find the current process poor, and to use that figure to justify expanding the release scope. Work out what the numbers actually support before the meeting.

blanks.label: Response rate, as a percentage to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Fifty-four replies out of 240 staff is 22.5 percent. More than three quarters of the population said nothing at all, and nothing in the survey tells you what they think.

blanks.label: Percentage of all 240 staff who both replied and rated the process poor, to one decimal place
blanks.rationale: Forty-two out of 240 is 17.5 percent. That is the largest claim the data supports about the whole workforce, and it is a quarter of the size of the figure proposed.

blanks.label: The 78 percent figure describes 78 percent of which group
