blanks.rationale: Forty-two of fifty-four is 78 percent of the people who answered, not of the staff. Naming the denominator is the difference between a defensible finding and a claim that collapses under the first question.

questions.explanation: A percentage is a claim about a population and it is only as good as the denominator attached to it. Low response is itself evidence about the channel and about who finds it worth answering, so the safe reading treats respondents as a self-selected group until something establishes otherwise. Quoting a proportion of the whole population from a partial sample is the fastest way to lose a steering group's trust in every other number you present.
questions.mindset: Name the denominator before you quote the percentage.

questions.stem: Your hospital wayfinding programme scores each stakeholder for power and for interest, both from 1 to 5, and multiplies the two to rank engagement effort. The estates director scores 5 for power and 1 for interest. The outpatient volunteer coordinator scores 1 for power and 5 for interest. They come out identical, and the PMO has proposed giving the two of them the same engagement treatment for the rest of the programme.

blanks.label: The product score each of the two stakeholders receives
blanks.rationale: Five multiplied by one is five in both cases. The arithmetic is identical precisely because multiplication discards which of the two factors was the large one.

blanks.label: Which of the two should be engaged with the aim of keeping them satisfied rather than closely informed
blanks.rationale: High power with low interest is the classic keep-satisfied position: he can stop the programme but does not want detail, so contact is infrequent, senior and focused on what affects him.

blanks.label: The number of distinct quadrants the two occupy on a power and interest grid
blanks.rationale: They sit in opposite corners, high power with low interest and low power with high interest, which is why one ranking number cannot tell you how to treat either of them.

questions.explanation: Collapsing two dimensions into one number discards the direction of the score, and direction is what determines the engagement style. Ranking is useful for deciding how much attention a stakeholder gets, but the kind of attention follows which dimension is high: influence with little interest needs infrequent senior contact, while interest without influence needs generous information at low cost.
questions.mindset: Two stakeholders with the same score can still need opposite treatment.

questions.stem: The grid plots stakeholders by their power over your airport baggage system replacement and their interest in it. The head of security can stop go-live on safety grounds, has told you plainly that the project is not among his priorities this year, and has delegated attendance at your governance meetings to a junior officer. Select the quadrant where he belongs.

graphic.title: Power and interest grid with four quadrants, power on the vertical axis and interest on the horizontal
graphic.caption: Select a quadrant. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between quadrants, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: High power, low interest
regions.rationale: He holds an absolute veto and has said the project is not a priority, which is both dimensions stated explicitly. This is the quadrant that produces late, decisive intervention by someone who has not been following.

regions.label: High power, high interest
regions.rationale: This is where people place any stakeholder who feels important, upgrading interest to match power. His delegation of attendance is direct evidence against it, and the mistake leads to swamping him with detail he will not read.

regions.label: Low power, low interest
regions.rationale: Placing him here reads disengagement as unimportance. It is the most dangerous error on this grid, because the monitoring it implies is exactly enough to be surprised by a veto.

regions.label: Low power, high interest
regions.rationale: This inverts both readings. It fits someone who cares a great deal and can decide nothing, which is the opposite of a security head who can halt a go-live but has other priorities.

questions.explanation: Power describes what a stakeholder is able to do; interest describes what they currently choose to attend to. The two are assessed separately and a low reading on one must not be allowed to pull the other down with it. The cell holding high capability and low attention is where unpleasant surprises come from, because nothing in the day-to-day contact signals what that person could do at a gate.
questions.mindset: Assess what someone could do separately from what they currently care about.

questions.stem: The map shows who talks to whom around your open banking product. You need a decision from the partner bank's payments council, which meets monthly and has already deferred you twice. Your product owner deals with the bank's relationship manager, who is well connected across the commercial side but sits outside the council. Select the person whose support you should secure first.

graphic.title: Influence map showing your team, the bank's commercial group and the payments council, with the links between individuals
graphic.caption: Select a person. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between people, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Integration architect: sits in the bank's technical forum and attends the payments council as an adviser
regions.rationale: She is the only link between your side and the group that decides, and she is in the room when it does. A decision route runs through whoever bridges two otherwise separate clusters.

regions.label: Relationship manager: connected to your product owner and to four commercial staff
regions.rationale: He has the most connections on the map, which is why he is the usual answer. Every one of them is on a side that does not sit on the council, so his reach does not extend to the decision you need.

regions.label: Council chair: connected only to the other council members
regions.rationale: Going straight to the most senior node ignores the absence of any route to him. A cold approach to a chair arrives with nobody inside the room prepared to support it, which is how you get deferred a third time.

regions.label: Bank developer: works daily with two of your engineers
regions.rationale: This is the strongest and easiest relationship on the map, and it leads nowhere near the council. Choosing him mistakes the closeness of a tie for its usefulness to this particular decision.

questions.explanation: Influence travels along connections rather than down an organisation chart, so the useful question about any map is who bridges groups that would otherwise not reach each other. The node with the most links is usually well embedded in a single cluster, and the most senior node is usually reachable only through someone else. A broker converts an approach into an argument made inside the room by somebody the room already listens to.
questions.mindset: Look for who connects groups, not who is busiest inside one.
